ask.changes_what: New orthopnoea raises probability of decompensated HF and supports BNP/echo and decongestion; absence should not be used to exclude HF.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on the absence of orthopnoea to exclude heart failure, and do not attribute orthopnoea to heart failure without examining for tamponade, effusion or neuromuscular weakness when the picture does not fit.
ask.escalation_warning: Orthopnoea with hypotension, pulsus paradoxus or a raised JVP suggests tamponade or acute pump failure; obtain immediate echo.

evidence.citation: Fonseca C, Morais H, Mota T, et al. The diagnosis of heart failure in primary care: value of symptoms and signs. Eur J Heart Fail. 2004;6(6):795-800.
evidence.population: Portuguese primary care attendees screened by Boston questionnaire and referred for echocardiography (n=1058 assessed); orthopnoea sensitivity reported only as <36%
evidence.quote: a history of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (LR 35.5), orthopnea (LR 39.1) and breathlessness when walking on the flat (LR 25.8)
evidence.reference_standard: Resting echocardiography with clinical assessment
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (cardiac dysfunction at rest on echocardiography)

evidence.citation: Ekundayo OJ, Howard VJ, Safford MM, et al. Value of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and medications in prospective population studies of incident heart failure. Am J Cardiol. 2009;104(2):259-264.
evidence.population: 5,771 community-dwelling adults >=65 years in the Cardiovascular Health Study; 272 with adjudicated definite HF
evidence.quote: for either orthopnea or PND were 52% (95% confidence interval [CI] 46% to 58%), 83% (95% CI 82% to 84%)
evidence.reference_standard: Centrally adjudicated definite heart failure (CHS criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Prevalent definite heart failure (composite symptom: orthopnoea OR paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)

ask.how: Ask whether breathing worsens within minutes of lying flat and eases on sitting up, how many pillows (or what head-of-bed angle) are needed to sleep, and whether this is new or increased compared with baseline. Distinguish from positional dyspnoea due to abdominal distension, obesity, or nasal obstruction, and from cough-related waking.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of orthopnoea only modestly lowers the probability of heart failure; many heart failure patients, particularly with chronic disease, sleep flat.
ask.pitfalls: Orthopnoea also occurs with COPD, massive ascites, obesity, and bilateral diaphragm paralysis; pillow count is confounded by habit, reflux and sinus disease. In chronic HF orthopnoea correlates poorly with measured wedge pressure.
ask.positive_finding: New or worsening need to sleep propped up, with dyspnoea on lying flat that resolves on sitting, points to raised left-sided filling pressure (heart failure) or, less often, tamponade, large effusion or bilateral diaphragm weakness.
ask.prerequisites: Patient (or collateral historian) able to describe sleep position and recent change.
ask.rationale: Orthopnea helps distinguish acute heart failure from other causes of dyspnea and guides early management.
ask.title: Orthopnea: dyspnea lying flat relieved by sitting up / number of pillows

ask.changes_what: Positive: de-emphasize ACS and work up PE/pneumonia/pneumothorax/pericarditis (exam, CXR, PE risk score). Negative: does not remove PE from the differential.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pleuritic quality to discharge a patient with possible ACS without an ECG and troponin.
ask.escalation_warning: Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling or hemoptysis warrants immediate PE work-up; with sudden dyspnea consider pneumothorax.

evidence.quote: pleuritic chest pain (LR, 0.2)
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed MI by study criteria (enzymes/ECG) in included studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute myocardial infarction

Clinical features from the history and physical examination that predict the presence or absence of pulmonary embolism in symptomatic emergency department patients: results of a prospective, multicenter study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):307-315.
evidence.population: 7,940 symptomatic US ED patients tested for PE (12 centers); mean age 49, 67% female
evidence.quote: those with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.5 included non-cancer-related thrombophilia (OR 1.99), pleuritic chest pain (OR 1.53)
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging-confirmed PE or DVT within 45 days
evidence.target_condition: Venous thromboembolism (PE or DVT) in ED patients evaluated for PE

ask.how: Ask whether the pain is sharp and clearly worse with a deep breath, cough or sneeze (not with exertion or palpation), and whether there has been any hemoptysis. Ask separately about onset, exertional relation and positional relief so the pleuritic quality is not conflated with other descriptors.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of pleuritic quality does not exclude PE, pericarditis or pneumonia; PE frequently presents with isolated dyspnea or collapse without pleuritic pain.
ask.pitfalls: Pleuritic pain lowers but does not exclude ACS; no history element alone permits discharge without testing. Patients may label any sharp pain as breath-related unless asked specifically about inspiration.
ask.positive_finding: Pleuritic pain lowers the probability of myocardial infarction (LR about 0.2) and shifts the differential toward pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pleural disease. In ED patients evaluated for PE it modestly raises VTE probability (adjusted OR 1.5).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask before analgesia if feasible.
ask.rationale: Pleuritic chest pain supports PE or pneumonia and would shift workup toward imaging and anticoagulation.
ask.title: Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with inspiration/cough), +/- hemoptysis

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis, prevalence by Wells clinical probability category

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: VTE risk factors are critical for PE probability and immediate diagnostic and therapeutic decisions.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: SBP <90/MAP <65: resuscitate, lactate, POCUS (RUSH) to classify shock type, cause-directed therapy now. Normal BP: keep looking for compensated shock (HR, lactate, mentation, urine output).
examine.contraindications: Avoid the arm with a dialysis fistula, lymphoedema or recent axillary surgery; none otherwise.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a single normal cuff reading to exclude shock or tamponade; do not interpret SBP <90 as 'baseline' without documented prior values.
examine.escalation_warning: SBP <90 or MAP <65 with altered mentation, lactate >2, oliguria or cool skin is shock: immediate resuscitation and senior/ICU review; in suspected dissection or tamponade, hypotension signals imminent collapse.

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical examination for acute aortic dissection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2019.
evidence.population: Pooled 4 studies of ED patients evaluated for suspected acute aortic dissection (review total 9 studies, 2,400 participants; prevalence range 21.9-76.1%)
evidence.quote: hypotension (n = 4, specificity = 95%, LR+ = 2.9 95% CI = 1.8-4.6, I2 = 42%)
evidence.reference_standard: Acute aortic dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery or autopsy per primary studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection; finding = hypotension as defined by each primary study (thresholds varied; not uniformly SBP <90 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Drazner MH, Hellkamp AS, Leier CV, Shah MR, Miller LW, Russell SD, Young JB, Califf RM, et al. Value of clinician assessment of hemodynamics in advanced heart failure: the ESCAPE trial. Circ Heart Fail. 2009.

evidence.population: 188 patients hospitalised with advanced decompensated HF in the ESCAPE trial with pulmonary artery catheter measurements
evidence.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
evidence.target_condition: Low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = SBP <90 mmHg on baseline examination

evidence.citation: Guberman BA, Fowler NO, Engel PJ, Gueron M, Allen JM. Cardiac tamponade in medical patients. Circulation. 1981.
evidence.population: 56 medical patients with cardiac tamponade, single-centre case series, University of Cincinnati
evidence.quote: heart sounds were diminished in 19 patients; arterial systolic pressure was greater than or equal to 100 mm Hg in 35
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/haemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade with relief by pericardiocentesis or pericardial resection
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (sensitivity only); finding = systolic BP <100 mmHg (threshold differs from id title's <90)

examine.how: Measure with a correctly sized cuff on a supported arm (manual if the automated reading is doubtful or the pulse is irregular), repeat, and measure both arms when dissection is possible; calculate MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP)/3. Interpret against the patient's usual pressure and drug list.
examine.negative_finding: A normal SBP does not exclude shock (compensated haemorrhage, early sepsis, cardiogenic shock with vasoconstriction) or tamponade (about 60% of tamponade patients had SBP ≥100), nor low cardiac index in heart failure (SBP <90 sensitivity 12%).
examine.pitfalls: Chronic hypertensives are hypoperfused at 'normal' pressures; beta-blockers, pacemakers and automated cuffs in AF mislead. Interarm difference >20 mmHg raises dissection concern. Cuff readings overestimate true pressure in profound vasoconstriction.
examine.positive_finding: SBP <90 (or MAP <65) is shock until proven otherwise and should trigger a search for the cause (septic, hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, cardiogenic, obstructive: tamponade/PE/tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, adrenal). In suspected dissection, hypotension roughly triples the odds (LR+ 2.9, specificity 95%). It is not a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Appropriate cuff size; awareness of baseline BP, beta-blockers/antihypertensives and pacing.
examine.rationale: Documented hypotension requires immediate resuscitation and narrows the differential toward shock states.
examine.title: Systolic BP <90 mmHg (or MAP <65) at the bedside

examine.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
examine.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.

evidence.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
evidence.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
evidence.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
evidence.reference_standard: Right heart catheterization (PCWP >= 18 mmHg)
evidence.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).
evidence.population: Adults with a new episode of acute dyspnea; 8 ED studies, 4737 patients; HF prevalence 25-59%
evidence.quote: Elevated jugular venous pressure (0.88, pooled odds ratio: 7), added third heart sound (0.97), and lung crepitations (0.77, pooled odds ratio: 11)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea

evidence.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
evidence.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; individual patient data meta-analysis of 9 studies
evidence.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care

examine.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
examine.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
examine.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
examine.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
examine.rationale: Elevated JVP helps differentiate cardiogenic from hypovolemic or distributive shock in acute dyspnea.
examine.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative

examine.changes_what: Bibasilar crackles favor HF (add JVP, S3, BNP/POCUS); focal crackles with fever favor pneumonia (CXR); clear lungs do not rule out either but lower HF probability modestly.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use clear lungs to exclude heart failure in chronic HF patients (crackles are often absent with high filling pressures) or to exclude pneumonia in the elderly/immunocompromised, where auscultation is insensitive.
examine.escalation_warning: Diffuse crackles with hypoxemia and hypotension suggest pulmonary edema from cardiogenic shock or ARDS and require immediate escalation regardless of etiology.

evidence.quote: rales (negative LR = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.37-0.70)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/echo-based HF diagnosis per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Congestive heart failure as cause of dyspnea (absence of rales)

evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea (lung crepitations/rales)

evidence.citation: Htun TP, Sun Y, Chua HL, Pang J. Clinical features for diagnosis of pneumonia among adults in primary care setting: a systematic and meta-review. Sci Rep 2019;9:7600.
evidence.population: Adults >=18 without serious illness or immunosuppression presenting to primary care/outpatient/emergency clinics with respiratory symptoms; 13 studies, 11,144 participants; pneumonia prevalence 5-50%
evidence.reference_standard: Chest radiograph
evidence.target_condition: Radiographic community-acquired pneumonia (crackles present)

evidence.citation: Marchello CS, Ebell MH, Dale AP, Harvill ET, Shen Y, Whalen CC. Signs and symptoms that rule out community-acquired pneumonia in outpatient adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Am Board Fam Med 2019;32(2):234-47.
evidence.population: Outpatient adults/adolescents with acute respiratory infection; 3 studies; baseline CAP risk ~4%
evidence.quote: had a summary estimate of LR- of 0.10 (95% CI, 0.07 to 0.13) with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.92
evidence.reference_standard: Chest radiograph
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia; COMPOSITE rule-out = normal vital signs AND normal pulmonary examination (no crackles or other auscultatory abnormality)

examine.how: With the patient sitting, auscultate posterior bases and all fields during slow deep breaths through an open mouth, comparing sides. Have the patient cough before calling crackles persistent; note timing (late-inspiratory fine = edema/fibrosis; coarse = secretions), distribution (bibasilar symmetric vs focal), and whether they clear with position change.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of crackles lowers the probability of heart failure only moderately (LR- 0.35-0.51) and does not exclude pneumonia; normal vital signs plus a normal lung examination together make CAP unlikely (LR- 0.10).
examine.pitfalls: Dependent-atelectasis crackles clear with deep breaths or cough; chronic 'velcro' crackles of fibrosis mimic edema; in chronic HF crackles are often absent despite high wedge pressure, and obese or shallow-breathing patients give false negatives.
examine.positive_finding: Bibasilar symmetric late-inspiratory crackles in an acutely dyspneic adult raise the probability of heart failure (pooled specificity ~0.77-0.81); focal/unilateral crackles with fever or cough raise the probability of pneumonia (pooled LR+ ~2.4). Crackles are non-specific and also occur in ILD, atelectasis, COPD and bronchiectasis.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, diaphragm on skin, patient able to take deep breaths; re-listen after several deep breaths because dependent atelectasis crackles clear.
examine.rationale: Crackles can rapidly distinguish heart failure from PE or pneumonia and guide urgent therapy.
examine.title: Pulmonary crackles: bibasilar (heart failure) vs focal/unilateral (pneumonia)

examine.changes_what: Muffled sounds with hypotension/JVP elevation: immediate bedside echo for effusion; normal sounds: no reassurance - image if tamponade is otherwise plausible.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of muffled sounds to exclude tamponade, and do not use the sign alone to diagnose it.
examine.escalation_warning: Muffled sounds with hypotension, raised JVP or pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg = suspected tamponade: emergent echocardiography and preparation for pericardiocentesis.
examine.how: Auscultate the apex and left sternal border in a quiet room with the patient supine and then leaning forward; judge whether S1/S2 are distant or muffled relative to what the chest-wall thickness would predict, and compare with prior exams if available. Look concurrently for JVP elevation, hypotension and pulsus paradoxus.
examine.negative_finding: Normal heart sounds do not exclude a pericardial effusion or tamponade, particularly in rapidly accumulating (traumatic, post-procedural) effusions.
examine.pitfalls: Highly subjective and setting-dependent; noisy EDs, hyperinflated chests and large body habitus all diminish sounds. Do not wait for the full Beck triad before obtaining echocardiography.
examine.positive_finding: Distant heart sounds with hypotension and raised JVP (Beck triad) suggest tamponade, but the triad is present in only a minority of tamponade cases; diminished sounds alone are common in COPD/hyperinflation, obesity and pleural effusion.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet environment; a baseline examination greatly improves the judgement of 'diminished'.
examine.rationale: Muffled heart sounds in hypotension raise concern for tamponade, prompting urgent echo and intervention.
examine.title: Muffled/diminished heart sounds (Beck triad component)

Muffled heart sounds in hypotension raise concern for tamponade, prompting urgent echo and intervention.
